newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asian Grains - S.Korea to buy more Chinese corn.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grains - S.Korea to buy more Chinese corn.

text.p: South Korean buyers estimate China may have a further half a million tonnes of corn on offer after domestic feedmills embarked on a buying spree picking up 250,000 tonnes of Chinese origin, traders said on Monday.
Japanese buyers, who have covered 90 percent of their April/June corn requirements, may also buy Chinese corn soon in place of U.S. grain.
"Chinese corn is much more attractive than U.S. corn because its cheaper and we can get it faster," a trader with a Seoul-based foreign trading house said.
The Chinese corn bound for South Korea will be for shipment between June to September to take advantage of shorter shipping periods and smaller cargoes, traders said.
"Chinese corn also lets us easily manage our feed grain inventory in factories," one said.
Since January, South Korean buyers have bought at least 564,000 tonnes of Chinese corn and China may still have half a million tonnes of corn available for export, they added.
"China is now offering corn at a slightly cheaper price, compared with prices of U.S. corn. Some Japanese traders are seeking to buy Chinese corn," one trader in Tokyo said.
He estimated that Chinese corn is now some US$3-$4 a tonne lower compared with that of U.S. corn.
"Domestic buyers have been looking for Chinese corn not only for smaller vessels suitable for minor ports but also for Panamax-size vessels for major ports," the trader said.
"Unless U.S. corn premiums fall significantly, Japanese buyers will increasingly switching to other origins such as Chinese corn and corn of South American-origins," another trader in Japan said.
U.S. corn premiums were quoted flat in Japan at about 97 U.S. cents a bushel over the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) May contract.

In Taiwan, traders expect to see two tenders this week for 54,000 tonnes of soybeans and 54,000 tonnes of corn. The Taiwan Flour Mills Association also plans to tender on Thursday for two shipments totalling 69,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat, traders said.

Taiwanese and Japanese traders expressed concerns over the forthcoming United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) March 11 crop report and talk of rain damaging the Brazilian soybean crop, which may boost already high soybean and soy product prices even further.
Taiwanese dealers expect the USDA to reduce its 1996-97 soybean ending stocks to around 135 million bushels, down from earlier reports of 140 million bushels.
"If the USDA estimate falls below 130 million bushels, soybean futures will test the 840 U.S. cents upper resistance," a soybean buyer in Taiwan said.

Japanese traders have delayed their soybean purchases as they await Tuesday's USDA report, but said they also feared soybean inventories would be downwardly revised putting further upward pressure on global prices.
Taiwanese buyers current heavy rains in Brazilian soybean growing areas may damage the crop giving another twist to any upward spiral.
"The rain in Brazil will damage crops if it continues for a while," one buyer said.
Argentine corn and Brazilian soybeans will remain attractive for Taiwanese buyers who are seeking alternatives to rising U.S. corn and soybeans prices, traders said.

Taiwan buyers would consider buying Argentine corn if prices were $5.00 a tonne below those of U.S. corn. Brazilian soybeans would be considered if prices were $10 a tonne below that of U.S. soybeans, they said.
Meanwhile, Japanese importers have started buying U.S. soybeans for May shipment and premiums were quoted at about 115 U.S. cents a bushel over CBOT May futures.
Two Korean flour millers will also probably buy at least 21,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat this week for shipment in April-May to the port of Pusan, traders said.
They said local edible oil producers are also seeking 85,000 tonnes of U.S. No.2 soybeans for April shipment.
The Philippines, where one flour firm bought on Monday 40,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat, will be in the market for more supplies especially if prices dip further, traders there said.
Freight rates from the U.S. Pacific Northwest to South Korea were unchanged at around $14.50 a tonne and were also flat from the U.S. Gulf at $24.50 a tonne.
U.S. Gulf/Japan freight rates were little changed at around $25.50 a tonne for nearby shipments.

Taiwanese shipping sources quoted dry bulk rates from the U.S. Pacific Northwest at about $14.00 a tonne and from the Gulf of Mexico in a range between $24.50 and $25.00 a tonne, both for Panamax-sized March shipments.
